claims.text: The target material is an as-designed, high-performance multicomponent high-entropy alloy.
A controlled, optimized thermal treatment will reduce post-exposure toughness degradation.
The proposed intervention is an optimized thermal treatment.
The thermal treatment will stabilize the alloy's grain structure.
The thermal treatment will prevent deleterious phase transformations.
Grain structure is a mediator of the treatment's effect on toughness degradation.
Phase composition is a mediator of the treatment's effect on mechanical performance.
Stabilizing grain boundaries will reduce toughness degradation.
Preventing deleterious phase transformations will reduce toughness degradation.
The treatment is bounded to 500-800 °C for 1-10 hours under minimal or no external stress.
After heating, the treated alloy will retain its original strength-ductility combination.
After heating, the treated alloy will exhibit less toughness degradation than an untreated alloy.
The comparator is an untreated high-entropy alloy with identical composition and processing history.
Toughness, microstructure, and tensile properties can be compared between treated and untreated specimens.
Significantly lower toughness in the treated alloy than in the untreated baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
Any altered microstructure in the treated alloy relative to the untreated baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis expects treatment-induced stabilization of grain structure and phase composition, but the falsification rule says that any altered microstructure relative to the untreated baseline is falsifying. A microstructural alteration could instead be the intended mediator, so this criterion conflicts with the proposed mechanism.
